items.content:
The Army put me in charge of 46 soldiers, 15 vehicles, and $14 million in equipment when I was 23 years old. The Army had very high opinions of 23-year-olds.
Looking back, the most useful supply chain education I ever got wasn't my MBA.

It was the two years before it.

Some things the Army drilled into me that I still use managing multi-million dollar supplier networks today:

Logistics is leadership. In the field, when your supply line fails, the mission fails. Period. "We ran out" isn't a weather event — it's a planning failure. I brought that same standard to every procurement role I've had since. We don't run out. That's a decision, not a hope.

Plan for the worst case before it's the worst case. Military planning always starts with "what's the most dangerous thing that could happen" — and then works backwards. I do the same with supplier networks. If your most critical supplier called today and said they were shutting down: how long could you operate? If you don't know the answer, you haven't finished the planning.

Systems beat willpower. 46 people, 15 vehicles — I couldn't personally verify everything. I had to build checklists, accountability structures, and reporting systems that worked when I wasn't in the room. A supply chain that only works when the right person is watching it isn't a system. It's a dependency.

Communicate more than feels necessary. In the field, the most dangerous thing is someone who assumed instead of confirmed. I've watched million-dollar supplier problems start the same way — someone assumed a contract auto-renewed. Someone assumed the vendor knew about the spec change. Assume nothing. Confirm everything.

I've been out of the Army for 27 years. These four lessons still show up in some form every single week.

What's the most useful professional lesson you got from an unexpected place?
#SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement #Leadership

items.content:
A business student asked me for the single most important skill in procurement. I didn’t say negotiation. I didn’t say financial acumen. My answer surprised them.

I’ve been on the Penn State Behrend Black School of Business Advisory Board for a few years now, and every semester I get a version of the same question:

"What’s the most important skill I can have?"

My answer: Be able to drive who does what by when.

Not the answer they expect. But here’s why it’s the right one.

Procurement is at its heart a program management challenge. It doesn’t matter whether you’re timing in a new supplier, completing a new contract before the current one expires, or managing supplier compliance. Every one of these has gates and players that all need to move together.

That means leading internal and external stakeholders — making sure every one of them is talking to each other, establishing critical dates, and holding people accountable when those dates start to slip.

The best procurement leaders I’ve worked with aren’t the ones with the sharpest negotiation tactics. They’re the ones with clear systems to track commitments and the willingness to have the hard conversation when things fall behind. They’re velvet hammers — firm enough to keep the team moving at pace, skilled enough to do it without breaking relationships.

Without that discipline, nothing happens. The contract stalls. The qualification timeline drifts. The supplier misses a gate and nobody escalates until it’s a crisis.

When you drive the bus, you’re a lot less likely to be run over by it.

I tell the students: the skill isn’t the tactics. The skill is the willingness to keep people to their word.

The rest is just spreadsheets and phone calls.

What’s the best professional advice you’ve gotten that was different from what you expected?
#SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement

items.content:
Procurement is full of brilliant people who can't get their ideas heard.

It's not a knowledge problem.

It's an influence problem. 👇

❌ They have the right answer but can't get buy-in. 
❌ They know what needs to change but lack the authority to change it. 
❌ They're seen as a support function. Not a strategic one.

But the best procurement leaders I've worked with?

✅ Decisions get made differently when they're in the room. 
✅ They get buy-in without forcing it. 
✅ They move organisations. Without a mandate.

Most of them couldn't even tell you what they do differently. But watch them closely and there's a pattern.

Here's what they unknowingly do:

1. The 4C's Framework 

↳ Competence: demonstrate your expertise 
↳ Care: show you want the best for others 
↳ Character: lead with integrity 
↳ Consistency: be dependable in your actions

You cannot influence without trust. These four build it.

2. The S-C-Q-A Framework 

↳ Situation: what's the current state? 
↳ Complication: what's the challenge? 
↳ Question: what needs to be solved? 
↳ Answer: present your solution

Confident, clear communication builds trust. And it speeds up buy-in.

3. The 3 Pillars of Influence 

↳ Ethos (Credibility): consistent, competent, trustworthy 
↳ Pathos (Emotion): connect emotionally, understand their needs 
↳ Logos (Logic): use facts and data to strengthen your reasoning

The best influencers integrate all three. Especially when they don't have the formal authority.

4. Prioritise alliances over short-term consensus 

↳ Map your stakeholders: decision-makers, influencers, those affected 
↳ Pre-align your idea one-on-one with key stakeholders 
↳ Align objectives, share quick-wins, and publicly share credit 
↳ Co-ordinate messaging so allies present a united front

Alliances create momentum. They turn strong ideas into action.

5. The Principle of Reciprocity 

↳ Give before you ask 
↳ Share helpful resources 
↳ Support others' goals 
↳ Recognise contributions

People back those who have backed them.

Here's what most people miss.

Influence has nothing to do with where you sit in the hierarchy. It never has.

A CPO who doesn't understand these principles will struggle. 

A junior buyer who does will outperform people three levels above them.

Anyone can build this. At any level. If they understand the principles.

Start applying it wherever you are.

items.content:
We'd used the same logistics provider for years. Everyone loved them. Great service. Quick to help. Subject matter experts.
The holiday gift baskets weren't bad either.
Then we did a competitive bid. And found out what "good enough" was actually costing us.
Here's the thing about incumbents — they always get the benefit of the doubt. These are the people you've worked with for years. The teams know each other. The personalities mesh. You exchange Christmas cards. Nobody wants to be the person who disrupts a relationship that feels like it's working.
At one company, we'd been with the same local 3PL for years. They were deeply integrated into our process. I'd lost count of the number of times they'd swooped in to save a shipment that was lost or hung up in customs. They earned the loyalty. I'm not dismissing that.
But as we continued to grow, I knew we had to benchmark what we were paying and what we were getting. Not because we were unhappy. Because nobody had ever looked. It was something that always just was.
So I built a market basket of our actual shipments and started meeting providers — small local firms and the 500-lb behemoths of the industry. I created a feature matrix comparing what our incumbent provided against what else was available in the market.
What I found surprised me.
Online freight tracking. Spend analysis tools. Integrated warehousing. These weren't exotic capabilities. They were standard offerings from multiple providers — and we'd been operating without them for years because we never asked the question.
After narrowing the field, I let the incumbent know their business was up for bid. Showed them the matrix. Asked about the gaps. Gave them every chance to respond.
They couldn't close the gap.
We moved the business to a larger local 3PL. The result: 27% annual freight savings, better visibility, better tools, and a flawless transition.
The incumbent wasn't a bad company. They were a good company that had never been challenged — and a good relationship that had quietly become an expensive assumption.
Every company has one of these. A vendor, a process, a cost line that nobody questions because it's always been that way and the relationship feels fine.
"Fine" is the most expensive word in procurement.
What's the assumption in your supply chain that's costing you more than you think?
#SupplyChain #Procurement #Manufacturing #Logistics

items.content:
The most expensive supplier you have isn't the one charging you the most. It's the one your team is afraid to renegotiate with.
I've audited supplier relationships at six companies over 25 years.

The same pattern shows up every time.

There's always one or two vendors who've been "partners" for 10+ years. Long-tenured relationships. Senior contacts who maybe golf with someone at your company. Contracts that auto-renew because nobody wants to have the awkward conversation.

And almost without exception, those are the vendors who haven't had a meaningful pricing review in years.

The vendor you just onboarded last year? They got benchmarked, negotiated, and evaluated against alternatives. Their pricing is close to market.

The 12-year "partner"? Their margins are often 15-25% above market — protected by relationship, inertia, and the organizational myth that "the switching costs are too high."

Switching costs are real. I'm not dismissing them.

But the math on never having the conversation compounds year after year.

Here's what actually works:

Separate the relationship from the commercial review. "We value you as a long-term supplier. We also value market-rate pricing. Here's what comparable suppliers are charging."

Use data, not ultimatums. Show them where they sit against benchmark. Let the numbers do the talking so the conversation doesn't feel personal.

Give them the first chance to respond before going to market. Most long-term suppliers would rather reprice than lose the volume.

At Veza, we ran this exercise across our top 10 vendors. Achieved 4.6% cost reduction — without switching a single one of them.

The relationship survived. The pricing improved. Everybody left the table knowing where they stood.

When was the last time your longest-tenured supplier had a real pricing review?
#SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement

items.content:
The largest contract negotiation I ever led was $50 million over six years. Here’s the one thing that made the difference between a good deal and a great one.

GE Transportation needed motors. Millions of dollars of motors annually.

They’d always built them internally. This was the first time they were going external.

That meant finding a supplier willing to commit to six years of production and invest in the tooling to support it — while entering a commercial relationship with a customer who had massive volume leverage but also the accountability of a long-term dependency.

We came into that negotiation having done something most procurement teams don’t do: we spent three months before the first meeting building a detailed benchmark of what this motor supply should cost, what the tooling amortization should look like, and what the realistic cost reductions over the contract period were achievable.

We didn’t walk in with "we want the lowest possible price."

We walked in with the math.

Here’s why that matters: the supplier couldn’t argue with the benchmark. They could argue with our number — and they did — but they couldn’t argue with the methodology. We weren’t making up a target. We’d built the model.

The final contract: $50 million, six years, with $5.9 million in scheduled cost reductions built into the agreement.

The lesson I’ve carried from that negotiation:

The negotiator who walks in most prepared rarely has to fight hardest. The preparation does the work. The meeting is almost a formality.

What’s the most preparation you’ve ever done for a supplier negotiation?
#SupplyChain #Manufacturing #Procurement

Nobody throws a party when Procurement saves $500,000.
But they’ll break out the champagne when Sales closes a $500,000 deal. 

Here is the "Invisible Gap" that is costing your company more than you think, possibly 10x more.

The Cost Benefit Principle - 
Most C-suites understand this in theory, but almost none resource it like they believe it:
Save $1 in a negotiation - That full $1 goes straight to net profit.
Earn $1 in new revenue - Maybe $0.10 reaches the bottom line after commissions, delivery, and overhead.

The 5% Reality Check 
If your company operates on a 5% margin, the math gets even more punishing:
You need $2,000,000 in new sales to match the bottom-line impact of just $100,000 in procurement savings.

Let that land for a second.

"The money you save can be reinvested and create a significant competitive advantage for you and your company." Generate $500K sales vs Generate $500K sales, impact on the bottom line margin has a big difference.

items.content:
Most IBP redesigns add more structure. More meetings, more templates, more review cycles. Agile IBP does the opposite.

The monthly S&OP review stays. But it stops being the place where decisions are made. It becomes the place where decisions are confirmed, challenged, or escalated. The real work happens in smaller, faster loops in between.

What changes in practice:
The demand review stops being a forecast alignment meeting. It becomes a signal review. What has changed since last week, what does it mean for our decisions, and what do we not yet know.

The supply review stops being a capacity utilization report. It becomes a constraint conversation. Where are we exposed, what are the options, and what is the cost of each.

The executive meeting stops being a presentation of agreed numbers. It becomes a decision point for the scenarios that did not resolve themselves at a lower level.

The role of the IBP lead changes too. Less process owner, more decision architect. The job is not to run the meetings. It is to make sure the right tension reaches the right people at the right moment.

This is not a lighter process. It is a more intentional one.

#IntegratedBusinessPlanning #SupplyChain #DecisionArchitecture #PlanningExcellence #AgileIBP

items.content:
The planning system had all the data. Just not in a way anyone could use.

I worked on a supply chain project for a medical device business in North America. Three production sites. Components arriving from Europe and Asia. Everything maintained in SAP. But when the planning team needed to understand where parts were, when they would arrive, and in what quantity, SAP couldn't surface that in any practical way.

So we built a transparency layer in Excel. Not because we wanted to. Because the system wasn't designed for that business model. The SKU complexity, the multisite dependencies, the cross regional flows. SAP handled the transactions. It just couldn't give planners the view they needed to make decisions with confidence.

Once they had that view, things changed. Coordination between the European and North American teams improved. Escalation paths became clearer. Less firefighting, more forward planning. 

Service levels went from around 80 to above 90 percent.

What is the learning for me from that project is not only the result. It is the workaround. A global business running on spreadsheets sitting next to a system that cost tens of millions to implement.

Legacy ERP was built for a different era. Standardized processes, stable portfolios, predictable flows. When the business model gets more complex, the system rarely adapts. The organization does. Usually in Excel.

That gap is still there. In most companies I know, it never really closed.

What is changing now is the cost of closing it. With AI agents and lightweight custom tools, the workaround no longer has to be a spreadsheet. 

It can be something that actually fits the business model, connects to the data that matters, and surfaces the right decision at the right moment.

The technology is not the hard part anymore. Understanding what decision needs to be made, and by whom, still is.

#IntegratedBusinessPlanning #SupplyChain #ProcessExcellence #ERPTransformation

items.content:
Wir schauen oft auf den Bestand, wenn das eigentliche Problem längst sechs Wochen alt ist.

Der Bestand steigt. Die Lieferfähigkeit wird schlechter. Nach einer Störung braucht die Supply Chain erstaunlich lange, um wieder in einen stabilen Zustand zu kommen.

Dann beginnt die Suche.

War der Forecast falsch? Sind unsere Sicherheitsbestände zu hoch? Stimmen die Planungsparameter noch? Brauchen wir ein besseres System?

Alles berechtigte Fragen.

Aber ich frage mich zunehmend, ob wir damit nicht häufig zu spät ansetzen.
Denn die eigentliche Ursache liegt manchmal in einem Planungsmeeting Wochen zuvor.

Der Vertrieb sieht eine Chance im Markt. Supply hat Bedenken wegen Kapazitäten oder Lieferzeiten. Finance schaut auf Cash und Working Capital.
Jede Perspektive ist für sich nachvollziehbar.

Die Zahlen werden diskutiert, der Plan wird angepasst und irgendwann ein Forecast verabschiedet.

Was dabei erstaunlich oft unsichtbar bleibt, ist der Trade-off, den wir gerade akzeptiert haben.

Wenn wir diese zusätzliche Nachfrage absichern, was bedeutet das für unseren Bestand?

Wenn wir die Produktion heute reduzieren, wie schnell können wir bei einer Veränderung wieder reagieren?

Wenn wir die Lieferfähigkeit schützen, was passiert in den nächsten Wochen mit Cash und Marge?

Gerade in mittelständischen Pharmaunternehmen halte ich das für einen wichtigen Punkt.

Nicht jedes Planungsproblem braucht sofort Kinaxis. Und nicht jede Organisation muss erst ein dreijähriges SAP-Projekt durchlaufen, bevor bessere Entscheidungen möglich sind.

Vielleicht beginnt es an einer viel einfacheren Stelle:
Die Konsequenzen einer Planungsentscheidung sichtbar zu machen, solange man noch anders entscheiden kann.

Denn der Bestand ist nicht immer das Problem.
Manchmal ist er nur der Ort, an dem eine frühere Entscheidung endlich sichtbar wird.

#SupplyChain #IBP #Pharma #Mittelstand #DecisionMaking

Most IBP processes were designed to create alignment. What they often create instead is a very expensive consensus ritual.

Forecasts get negotiated. Numbers get smoothed. The uncomfortable scenarios disappear before they reach the meeting. And four weeks later, the market moves in exactly the direction nobody wanted to discuss.

I have been thinking about what it would mean to design IBP differently. Not lighter. Not faster. But genuinely built around decisions rather than around agreement.

What if the process started with the question: what do we not know yet, and how much does that uncertainty cost us? Instead of starting with the numbers everyone already agreed on.

There is a version of IBP that is less about monthly alignment and more about continuous decision readiness. Where scenarios are not a planning exercise but an actual operating mode. Where the process surfaces tension rather than removes it.

This is the conceptual foundation I am building KTP around. The conversations I am having suggest the problem is real and the appetite for something different is growing.

If this resonates, I would be curious what you are seeing in your organization.

items.content:
A few years ago, I ran a workshop with the commercial and finance teams at one of our European sales affiliates.

They had a real market opportunity on the table: a chance to drive a 30 to 40 percent demand increase within six months. On paper, it was a great business case. Higher forecast, stronger targets, more growth. From a commercial standpoint, going after it made total sense.

What they couldn't see from their side of the table was the actual supply chain behind that number. For this specific product, the full cycle, from API to bulk, semi finished, and finished goods, ran four to five years.

Increasing demand that fast wasn't just a matter of scaling up production. It meant pulling capacity from somewhere else. Another product. Another market. Another patient group.

Nobody was making that choice on purpose. It just happened over time, because nobody outside of supply chain could get a view of the global network constraints.

That workshop changed the dynamic for the whole team.

Once we put the lead times and production structures on the table, the questions changed. The commercial team didn't stop pushing for growth, nor should they, but the conversation became collaborative. Instead of just pushing a new number into the system, they started asking what was actually possible and what is the financial impact of these decisions.

This is where IBP earns its place beyond standard S&OP.

S&OP/IBP shouldn't be only a monthly forecasting exercise, and it definitely shouldn't be about supply chain saying "no" to sales. It is simply the moment where commercial ambition meets physical reality, before commitments are made, instead of after.

How visible is your supply chain network to the people setting your commercial targets?

items.content:
Finance wasn’t in the room when the decision was made. But they owned the consequences six weeks later.

A few weeks ago, I sat in a planning review with a pharma company. Finance and Supply Chain each had their own systems, their own numbers, and ultimately their own version of the truth.

During the meeting, Supply Chain shifted production priorities between two products to protect a critical customer commitment. Given the information available in the room, it was a reasonable decision.

Six weeks later, Finance saw the consequences during month end close. Margins were lower. Working capital was higher.

No one in the planning meeting had been able to see either impact before the decision was made. That wasn’t a poor decision. It was a system that could only reveal the consequences after they had already happened.

So we tried something simple. Before locking in a scenario, we added one question to the discussion.

What does this option do to margin? What does it do to cash? Not after the fact. Not in the monthly review. Right there, before the decision was made.

We didn’t build a sophisticated model. We simply introduced a rough estimate at the right moment. That alone changed two decisions during the first pilot.

I’ve seen the same pattern across many organisations. Operational decisions are made in one room. Financial consequences become visible in another.

By the time both perspectives come together, the decision has already become history.

I used to blame the software. After working with almost every leading planning tool across Pharma and FMCG, I am just not so sure anymore. 

They all do scenario planning. They all let you model an upside demand scenario and show you the supply gap.
But almost none of them tell you what the decision actually costs the business.

What does it mean for working capital? For margin? For cash? Finding that out usually requires a completely separate conversation, usually with Finance and usually weeks later.

The plan exists. The decision logic does not.

We keep waiting for better software to solve this, but maybe we are asking the wrong question. Was the planning process ever designed to answer financial questions in the first place? 

Most IBP cycles are built to consolidate supply and demand, not to surface the financial consequences of a choice.
That is not a software flaw. It is a decision design problem. And perhaps that explains why so many organizations invest millions into planning systems and still struggle with the same decisions.

The plan exists. The decision logic does not.

items.content:
We talk a lot about what AI agents can do.

But we are completely ignoring the real management challenge of the next decade: What happens when an agent and a human actually work on the same team?

Consider the friction points:
How does a critical handover work at 2 AM?
Who owns the outcome when an agent prepares a recommendation, but a human approves it?
What happens when algorithmic logic and human intuition point in different directions?
And how do you give feedback to a system that might repeat the exact same mistake at scale?

My view: We need to stop treating agents as just another software feature.
Not because they are employees. They are not. But because they require the exact same management discipline we expect when onboarding a new team member:

A clear role, defined responsibilities, decision boundaries, structured supervision and continuous feedback.

Because agents will make mistakes. They will work with incomplete information, misread context, and occasionally produce an answer that looks entirely convincing but is completely wrong.

The real test will not be whether an organization can avoid every failure. It will be whether it notices early enough, responds responsibly, and improves the system afterward.

That is why agentic AI is fundamentally an organizational design question.
Technology determines what an agent can do. Leadership determines what it should do, who remains accountable, and how humans and agents improve together over time.

The next decade is not just a race for better tech. It’s a test of whether our organizations are mature enough to work with it.

Where are you already seeing this tension in practice? Let’s discuss in the comments. 👇

#AIGovernance #Leadership #SupplyChain #FutureOfWork #OrganizationalDesign

The problem is not the forecast.

The other builds scenarios to make a decision before the situation forces one.

The difference is not the tool.

It is whether the scenario is connected to something that matters financially.

Margin at risk.
Cash exposure.
Working capital impact.

A scenario that does not answer “what would we do differently?” is just a chart with extra steps.

Conservative, base and upside scenarios side by side.
Connected to revenue, cost and inventory.

Not to replace existing planning systems. But to explore what a focused decision layer could look like on top of them.

items.content:
The planning system had all the data. Just not in a way anyone could use.

I worked on a supply chain project for a medical device business in North America. Three production sites. Components arriving from Europe and Asia. Everything maintained in SAP. But when the planning team needed to understand where parts were, when they would arrive, and in what quantity, SAP couldn't surface that in any practical way.

So we built a transparency layer in Excel. Not because we wanted to. Because the system wasn't designed for that business model. The SKU complexity, the multisite dependencies, the cross regional flows. SAP handled the transactions. It just couldn't give planners the view they needed to make decisions with confidence.

Once they had that view, things changed. Coordination between the European and North American teams improved. Escalation paths became clearer. Less firefighting, more forward planning. 

Service levels went from around 80 to above 90 percent.

What is the learning for me from that project is not only the result. It is the workaround. A global business running on spreadsheets sitting next to a system that cost tens of millions to implement.

Legacy ERP was built for a different era. Standardized processes, stable portfolios, predictable flows. When the business model gets more complex, the system rarely adapts. The organization does. Usually in Excel.

That gap is still there. In most companies I know, it never really closed.

What is changing now is the cost of closing it. With AI agents and lightweight custom tools, the workaround no longer has to be a spreadsheet. 

It can be something that actually fits the business model, connects to the data that matters, and surfaces the right decision at the right moment.

The technology is not the hard part anymore. Understanding what decision needs to be made, and by whom, still is.

#IntegratedBusinessPlanning #SupplyChain #ProcessExcellence #ERPTransformation

If it takes two weeks of alignment meetings to test one scenario, that is probably not a forecasting problem.

It is a design problem.

The question I took away from Basel is simple:

What does your organization actually do in the first four hours after a supply disruption?

article.subtitle: Tomaz Suklje

article.description: Honest field notes on AI agents, data quality, and the decisions nobody designs forBy John Kloetzing & Tomaz SukljeThis started as a quick catch-up be

items.content:
Launching a new product is one of the most complex planning moments in Pharma.

Not because data is missing. But because the trade-offs are real and costly, and everyone in the room has a different stake in the game.

I remember sitting in a launch alignment meeting where this exact friction escalated. Demand Planning wanted a 6-month safety stock because patient availability is non-negotiable. Finance saw millions in cash tied up in inventory that would expire if regulatory approval delayed by just two weeks.

Classic dead-end. The room was tense: not because people did not want to decide, but because the consequences of getting it wrong were visible to everyone.

What changed the game was not a sharper forecast. It was mapping out the trade-off explicitly before the vote.

Instead of fighting over who had the better crystal ball, we ran three scenarios side by side: conservative, base, upside. Each with its financial and operational consequences attached. Suddenly we were not debating assumptions. We were looking at what the business was actually prepared to accept.
That shift took the emotional pressure out of the room. It turned a standoff into a structured decision.

Scenario planning is not a methodology to me. It is a way to stay honest about uncertainty without letting it paralyse your operations.

Still refining the playbook. But when it clicks, the speed of execution is worth it.

How do you handle the cost vs. availability standoff during high-stakes launches?

#SupplyChain #IBP #ScenarioPlanning #PharmaOperations

Most S&OP reviews end with an updated forecast.

That is not always a failure of discipline.

Fewer are built to evaluate options for action.

Conservative.
Base.
Upside.

Cleanly modeled. Well presented.

What would we actually do differently in Scenario A compared to Scenario C?

Because the process did not require it.

A scenario without a decision consequence is not really a planning instrument.

It can easily become a way to show preparedness without forcing a choice.

For me, the difference between an S&OP process that plans and one that decides is not mainly in the model.

It is in the question asked before the meeting:

What are we prepared to do differently today, depending on what we see?

If that question is not on the agenda, the rest can become very polished conversation.

items.content:
A few years back, I managed a supply shortage on a blockbuster drug that dragged on for almost two years.

The supply issue itself was a headache, but what actually drained everyone was the politics. Every country wanted maximum supply, every sales team had a different priority, and because we lacked a shared decision structure, we were essentially renegotiating the rules of engagement every single Monday morning.

We finally broke the cycle by forcing three workstreams in parallel: one for manufacturing capacity, one for network safety stock, and one to manage the demand planning.

We didn’t do it because it was some brilliant strategy. We did it just to stop the fighting. Once the structure was there, the negotiation about the rules stopped, and the work of actually allocating supply began. The logic itself was secondary; what mattered was that the logic existed and everyone knew the game we were playing.

I’ve seen the same pattern everywhere since, not just in pharma. When supply gets tight, the bottleneck is rarely the effort or the capability. It’s almost always the absence of a decision architecture that everyone can point to.

It turns out that when things get chaotic, a clear set of rules is worth more than a perfect forecast.

AI can support this. But it will not replace leadership.

items.content:
An old product. No global priority. Limited investment. No reliable external supply base.

And yet, 50 to 60 percent of annual global demand depended on a single government tender in one country. The product was not the real problem.

The global organization treated it as a side issue. The local organization risked its reputation and its market presence every time delivery failed.

So, we built inventory.

Four to five million euros tied up in stock to protect a service level that was not globally prioritized, but was existential locally.

From a working-capital perspective, this looked incredibly difficult to justify.
From the local perspective, the alternative was impossible to justify.

This was not a planning failure. It was an alignment failure.

When global and local incentives are structurally misaligned, planning cannot produce a single, objectively "right" answer. It can only expose a conflict that leadership has yet to resolve.

Sometimes, excess inventory isn't the fundamental inefficiency.
The unresolved strategic objective is.

When did you last check whether your planning targets point in the same direction at every level?

items.content:
Last month in Basel, I had the chance to speak at a global supply chain conference and connect with practitioners from across the industry.

What stayed with me most was not my own presentation. It was the conversations afterwards.

Almost every discussion circled back to the same tension: we operate in a world where demand shifts fast, supply is fragile, and the pressure to stay resilient keeps growing. 

Most companies are responding by trying to build more flexibility into their operations. That makes sense.

But what came up repeatedly, and this felt like the real gap, is that we are not evolving our decision processes at the same speed.

Scenario planning, planning automation, AI. These topics came up in almost every conversation I had. Not as buzzwords. As genuine searches for answers.

The question that kept stopping people was not whether to act. It was where to start, and whether the ROI would justify it.

But I think the starting point is simpler than we make it: look at where your planning process breaks down under pressure. That is where the investment conversation becomes concrete.

Grateful for the exchange in Basel. These conversations are why this work matters.

#SupplyChain #IBP #ScenarioPlanning #PSIP2026

items.content:
Content creation doesn't have to feel lonely.

I started posting 4 years ago during COVID.

I built everything during lockdown, stuck behind a screen.

🔻Every connection was a DM.
🔻Every comment was a conversation.
🔻Every virtual call built a relationship.

Last year, I moved back to the UK, and it changed everything. 

One of those new connections, Fatima Khan, hosted an event in London.

80+ creators in that room.
No one needed introductions.
People already knew each other from here.
They'd spent months supporting each other online.
Now they were hugging like old friends for the first time.

That room validated all the work.

I wasn't posting into a void.
I was building bonds with people I just hadn't met yet.

Building a personal brand can be really lonely.

You WFH. 
Glued to your screen all day.
You post, close your laptop, and repeat.

Usually, people around you don't really understand what you're building.

That room reminded me that there are thousands of people on the same journey.

You just haven't met them yet.

So if you're worried you're talking into a void, here's what I'd do:

1. Comment on 5 creators' posts before yours
↳ Relationships start in comment sections long before DMs.

2. DM one creator each week
↳ Don't pitch them. Just say what you enjoyed.

3. Go to one creator event in your city
↳ One room can do what six months alone can't.

4. Start a group chat with 3-5 creators at your stage
↳ That becomes your accountability board before you publish.

5. Stop treating LinkedIn like an audience
↳ Trust is earned one interaction at a time.

Your audience lives online.
Your community turns up in person.

What creator here has become a genuine friend?
Tag them below. 

♻ Repost this if it helped.

"Hi LinkedIn Support, I am writing to vouch for Fatima Khan (fatima-rasheed-khan), case number 260723-029352.

Fatima is a legitimate creator with over 100,000 followers and her account is central to her business. She cannot regain access because the Persona identity verification repeatedly fails with a 'Can't verify photos' error.

Last Thursday, LinkedIn removed my account. 

110k+ followers, 500+ posts. All gone.

I kept it quiet, and simply raised a ticket. 

But then the messages started flooding in: "Are you okay?" "What happened to your profile?"

I honestly didn't think anyone would care. 

Almost gave up trying to get it back.

But so many people messaged showing their support.

Yesterday, Charlie posted asking people to help. It reached:

- 40,000 impressions in just 6 hours! 
- 100s of people raised a ticket on my behalf.
- #Bringbackfatima was everywhere in the comments.

The support was unreal & it helped get my account back.

A huge thank you to LinkedIn's creator team too.

This experience reminded me why I started Link Creators Club.

Creators need to be brought together! 

There’s an army of us working in isolation. 

We’re so much more powerful together vs on our own.

- Meet your LinkedIn connections IRL.
- Take chats in the DMs from comments.
- Build connections “outside of LinkedIn” too. 

That is where the real power is. 

I cannot wait to bring together all the UK creators on 11th September again.

Thank you to everyone who showed support.

I see you. I appreciate you. 🩵
